methodology.scope: Causal forensic completion for five representative L1 dossiers that had descriptive synthesis rows but no shared forensic-analysis contract.
methodology.observation_rule: Volatile DefiLlama figures were fetched in one sequential API run beginning at 2026-08-03T17:15:40.082Z. Each case preserves the exact returned values, historical-point date, peak basis, and method in forensic_analysis.observation_snapshot because same-day provider values can be revised. Metrics are observations, not proof that a design choice caused an outcome. Protocol and foundation sources establish documented mechanics, decisions, incidents, and stated strategy; they are not independent validation of adoption or performance.
methodology.preservation_rule: Migration 0073 adds forensic_analysis to synthesis and review metadata to _meta. It does not replace the existing identity, token, capital, onchain, team, narrative, risk, links, or legacy synthesis fields.
methodology.source_rule: Every assertion in outcome, why, strategic choices, counterfactual, and watch resolves to a checked source ID. Independent data tests the current outcome; primary sources establish the underlying decision or mechanism.
methodology.review_rule: All five records were reviewed on 2026-08-03 and are scheduled for another review on 2026-08-10 because their market, product, upgrade, and governance evidence changes quickly.

outcome.label: successful
outcome.summary: Stellar is a successful specialist settlement network, not a broad smart-contract winner. In the DefiLlama API snapshot fetched at 2026-08-03T17:15:40.082Z, the latest 2026-08-03 historical point was $214.2 million of DeFi TVL, with roughly $890.7 million of dollar stablecoins, $35.4 million of 30-day DEX volume, $2.93 million of 30-day fees, and $226,657 of 30-day revenue. Those observations show a live payment and issuance base 12.2% below its TVL peak, while the much smaller DEX and revenue figures keep the outcome below a claim of category-wide dominance. Same-day provider values may revise after the stated retrieval time.

why.summary: Observed: Stellar retains a large stablecoin base, TVL close to its June 2026 peak, and recurring fees, while its DEX activity and retained revenue are much smaller. Documented design: it made issued assets, trustlines, payment operations, anchors, low XLM resource requirements, and safety-first federated consensus first-class long before adding general smart contracts. Strategic inference: that sequencing created a durable distribution niche around payments and regulated issuance without requiring Stellar to win the EVM liquidity race. Adding Rust/Wasm contracts later lets those classic assets enter programmable workflows without discarding their issuer controls. The trade-off is structural: issuer and anchor dependence remains offchain, SCP quorum choices can stop liveness, and strong stablecoin settlement does not automatically create large XLM or protocol-revenue capture.

strategic_choices.decision: Use federated Byzantine agreement with validator-selected quorum sets instead of proof of work or token-weighted proof of stake.
strategic_choices.consequence: Stellar avoids mining and validator-reward economics and prioritizes safety over liveness, but operators must configure intersecting quorums correctly; the 2019 halt demonstrated that configuration failures can stop the network even when safety holds.

strategic_choices.decision: Build native asset issuance, trustlines, exchange, and anchor standards into the payment rail before offering general smart contracts.
strategic_choices.consequence: Issuers and payment businesses received lower-complexity primitives and redemption integrations, helping Stellar retain a stablecoin niche; users still depend on each issuer or anchor for reserves, authorization, and offchain redemption.

strategic_choices.decision: Add Soroban Rust/Wasm contracts through a later protocol rollout and make classic assets accessible through the Stellar Asset Contract.
strategic_choices.consequence: Stellar can extend a mature payment ledger into programmable finance without replacing its existing asset system, while inheriting a newer contract-state and storage failure surface illustrated by the archival incident.

strategic_choices.decision: Keep XLM focused on fees, rent, and minimum balances rather than making every issued asset settle economically through XLM.
strategic_choices.consequence: Applications can move dollar and other issuer assets cheaply without taking native-token price risk, but payment or stablecoin growth need not translate proportionally into XLM demand or protocol revenue.

counterfactual.summary: Launching EVM-compatible general contracts earlier might have attracted more portable DeFi liquidity and developers, but it would also have exposed the young payment network to a larger application, state, and exploit surface before its issuance rails matured. Retaining only classic payment operations would have reduced Soroban-specific complexity but capped programmability. The reviewed sources do not establish that either path would have produced more durable usage, and the 2025 archival failure shows the real cost of the added state machinery rather than proving the expansion was a mistake.

watch.signal: Stablecoin supply, TVL, DEX volume, fees, and retained revenue tracked separately.
watch.implication: Growth across settlement and revenue would show that payment distribution is converting into a broader economy; stablecoins rising without fees or revenue would preserve the value-capture gap.

watch.signal: Independent quorum-set, Tier-1 validator, issuer, and anchor concentration measurements plus any new liveness incident.
watch.implication: More independent control would strengthen the safety-and-resilience thesis; concentrated trust or another configuration halt would weaken it.

watch.signal: Soroban application usage and state-integrity incidents after the archival fixes.
watch.implication: Sustained contract use without repeated state failures supports the late-programmability strategy; recurring corruption would show that expansion added more risk than durable demand.

unknowns.question: Who ultimately controls the quorum sets and infrastructure relied upon by the largest validators?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A current independent entity-level quorum and hosting analysis.

unknowns.question: How concentrated are stablecoin supply, payment volume, and redemption capacity by issuer and anchor?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: Issuer-level balances, flows, redemption terms, and independently verified reserve coverage.

unknowns.question: What share of Soroban usage persists without grants or temporary incentives?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: Public application cohorts, fee attribution, and incentive-adjusted retention.

unknowns.question: How much network growth creates incremental XLM demand rather than only demand for issued assets?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A reproducible decomposition of fees, rent, minimum balances, circulating float, and application asset demand.

outcome.label: middling
outcome.summary: Sui is a technically differentiated but middling L1. In the DefiLlama API snapshot fetched at 2026-08-03T17:15:40.082Z, the latest 2026-08-03 historical point was $417.2 million TVL, 84.2% below its October 2025 peak, alongside roughly $432.0 million of dollar stablecoins, $791.9 million of 30-day DEX volume, $4.86 million of 30-day fees, and $710,636 of 30-day revenue. That is meaningful current activity, but the deep capital drawdown and four officially documented halt or stall incidents across January and May 2026 prevent a stronger outcome call. Same-day provider values may revise after the stated retrieval time.

why.summary: Observed: Sui still processes substantial DEX volume and fees, but TVL is more than 84% below peak and official reports document a January stall and three May halt incidents. Documented design: Sui rejected EVM compatibility for an object-centric Move model, distinguished owned objects from shared objects, and built first-party consumer, liquidity, storage, wallet, and developer infrastructure around that architecture. Strategic inference: this gives asset-heavy applications a coherent concurrency and ownership model that competitors cannot reproduce with a thin compatibility layer, but it also makes Sui responsible for a novel stack whose correctness and distribution must mature together. Foundation-managed token releases and vertical product support accelerate bootstrapping, yet obscure how much liquidity and usage are independent of allocations, incentives, and first-party infrastructure.

strategic_choices.decision: Reject EVM compatibility and make Sui Move plus object ownership the execution model.
strategic_choices.consequence: Owned objects can support direct, asset-oriented execution and stronger language-level constraints, while developers and liquidity cannot migrate through ordinary EVM tooling and the novel model must earn its own ecosystem.

strategic_choices.decision: Separate owned-object transactions from shared-object consensus to pursue low latency and parallel execution.
strategic_choices.consequence: The architecture can avoid unnecessary coordination for independent assets, but interactions touching shared state still require consensus and the larger set of execution paths increases implementation and restart-state complexity.

strategic_choices.decision: Vertically support liquidity, wallet, storage, gaming, and consumer infrastructure instead of limiting the original contributor and Foundation to the base protocol.
strategic_choices.consequence: Integrated products can reduce cold-start friction and make the differentiated object model usable, while first-party breadth creates neutrality, dependency, and attribution questions when ecosystem activity is evaluated.

strategic_choices.decision: Release most of the capped 10 billion SUI supply over time through Foundation-managed schedules and ecosystem programs.
strategic_choices.consequence: The reserve can fund validators, builders, and distribution, but the schedule is explicitly adjustable to network needs, leaving future float, incentive dependence, and Foundation allocation power material to the outcome.

counterfactual.summary: An EVM-compatible path would have lowered developer and liquidity switching costs, but it would have surrendered much of the object-ownership differentiation Sui was created to test. A narrower base-protocol role might reduce first-party dependency, while slowing the wallets, liquidity, storage, and consumer products needed to demonstrate the architecture. More conservative upgrade sequencing or stronger failure containment could plausibly have reduced 2026 liveness incidents, but the postmortems do not quantify what delivery speed or functionality would have been sacrificed.

watch.signal: TVL, stablecoins, DEX volume, fees, and revenue after Foundation and application incentives are separated where possible.
watch.implication: Capital and revenue retention without subsidies would support a durable object-model economy; volume without recovering capital or revenue would keep the chain middling.

watch.signal: Frequency, duration, and blast radius of future liveness incidents after the May 2026 containment work.
watch.implication: A long incident-free period would show the novel stack is maturing; another input- or restart-triggered halt would weaken the reliability thesis.

watch.signal: Actual circulating supply, Foundation deployments, validator stake concentration, and adjustments to the published release path.
watch.implication: Transparent, broadly distributed releases reduce overhang and control risk; discretionary or concentrated deployment preserves both.

unknowns.question: How much Sui liquidity and user retention survives after grants, emissions, and trading incentives are removed?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: Incentive-adjusted application cohorts, liquidity, volume, fees, and revenue.

unknowns.question: Who beneficially controls validator stake and Foundation delegations?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A current independent entity-level stake and operator map.

unknowns.question: How much activity depends on Mysten- or Foundation-supported products and infrastructure?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: Attributable usage and revenue by independent versus affiliated applications and services.

unknowns.question: Will post-May failure containment prevent a single malformed input or restart-state bug from halting the network again?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: Published remediation verification plus sustained production evidence or a contrary incident.

outcome.label: middling
outcome.summary: Near is a middling L1 whose strongest current signal comes from cross-chain execution rather than native capital depth. In the DefiLlama API snapshot fetched at 2026-08-03T17:15:40.082Z, the latest 2026-08-03 historical point was $60.1 million TVL, 87.5% below its May 2022 peak, alongside roughly $128.7 million of dollar stablecoins, $2.53 billion of 30-day DEX volume, $3.16 million of 30-day fees, and $558,558 of 30-day revenue. NEAR's own revenue dashboard reports additional Intents economics, but that operator-controlled series is not treated as independent proof of durable demand. Same-day provider values may revise after the stated retrieval time.

why.summary: Observed: Near combines comparatively thin native TVL with very high tracked 30-day DEX volume and measurable fee revenue. Documented strategy: it moved from competing primarily as a sharded, developer-friendly L1 to treating chain fragmentation as the product problem, using Chain Signatures, solver-filled Intents, and a 2026 roadmap centered on cross-chain finance and autonomous agents. Strategic inference: the pivot gives Near a differentiated distribution surface that can route activity across other chains without requiring all assets or users to migrate to Near first. It also makes success harder to attribute: volume can pass through Intents while liquidity, execution, and value remain elsewhere, and the system adds solver, bridge, MPC, relayer, and potentially TEE dependencies. The current activity validates a working product, not yet a proven durable moat or complete NEAR-token capture mechanism.

strategic_choices.decision: Build a sharded Wasm L1 with account-level usability features instead of starting as an EVM-compatible chain.
strategic_choices.consequence: Near gained a distinct scaling and developer architecture, but had to build its own liquidity and tooling network effects; later compatibility and abstraction layers became necessary to reach users and assets elsewhere.

strategic_choices.decision: Reframe the product from a destination L1 to chain abstraction, where users express outcomes and solvers compete to execute them.
strategic_choices.consequence: Near can serve demand without requiring users to understand or remain on its chain, producing substantial tracked cross-chain volume while weakening the simple assumption that product usage equals native TVL or token demand.

strategic_choices.decision: Use Chain Signatures and an MPC service so Near accounts and contracts can control addresses on external chains.
strategic_choices.consequence: Applications can coordinate native assets across heterogeneous chains without requiring a separate application contract on each one, while MPC operators, derivation logic, relayers, and external-chain execution become part of the security boundary.

strategic_choices.decision: Converge the 2026 roadmap around cross-chain finance and autonomous AI agents rather than maintaining a single L1-app narrative.
strategic_choices.consequence: The roadmap creates a distinctive agentic-commerce thesis and new potential distribution, but joins multiple unproven markets and makes it harder to determine whether usage is driven by durable user need, integrations, incentives, or narrative rotation.

counterfactual.summary: Remaining focused on native L1 applications and liquidity could have produced a simpler product story and clearer fee attribution, but would have forced Near to compete directly for users and capital against larger EVM and Solana ecosystems. The abstraction pivot sacrifices that simplicity for a chance to own cross-chain order flow. A bridge-only approach would be easier to reason about but would not provide solver competition or account-controlled signatures. The reviewed evidence cannot establish whether the current Intents volume would have appeared as native Near activity under a different strategy.

watch.signal: Independent Near DEX volume, fees, revenue, stablecoins, and TVL compared with the operator-controlled Intents revenue series.
watch.implication: Consistent cross-source growth and rising retained revenue would support the abstraction thesis; divergence or opaque attribution would weaken it.

watch.signal: Solver, interface, bridge, relayer, and MPC-operator concentration plus execution quality during stress.
watch.implication: Competitive routing and diverse control support the claimed abstraction layer; concentrated fulfillment or a correlated failure would reveal a hidden intermediary stack.

watch.signal: Delivery and sustained usage of the 2026 dynamic-sharding, confidential-execution, and agent roadmap outside first-party demonstrations.
watch.implication: Independent applications and recurring fees would convert the agentic thesis into evidence; roadmap delivery without retained users would not.

unknowns.question: What share of reported Intents and DEX volume is organic, repeated demand rather than routing loops, incentives, or a small number of integrations?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: Independent wallet cohorts, counterparty concentration, incentive-adjusted volume, and attributable fees.

unknowns.question: How much Intents revenue is retained for NEAR buybacks or burn after solver, interface, and partner payments?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: Reproducible onchain accounting reconciled by an independent data provider.

unknowns.question: Who controls the MPC, solver, relayer, bridge, and confidential-execution dependencies in practice?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: Current entity-level operator sets, thresholds, incident procedures, and independently tested exits.

unknowns.question: Will the AI-agent strategy create users and fees distinct from existing cross-chain trading?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: Auditable agent activity, paying customers, recurring tasks, and fee attribution outside promotional programs.

sources.title: Aptos staking, validator, and voter model

observation_snapshot.method: Single sequential API run using the latest historicalChainTvl point, provider-reported 30-day fee/revenue/DEX aggregates, and current stablecoinchains values. The historical TVL point is dated 2026-08-03 and can be revised after this retrieval time.

outcome.label: middling
outcome.summary: Aptos is a middling L1 with a large stablecoin footprint but weak capital retention and fee capture. In the DefiLlama API snapshot fetched at 2026-08-03T17:15:40.082Z, the latest 2026-08-03 historical point was $62.2 million TVL, 95.2% below its December 2024 peak, alongside roughly $1.18 billion of dollar stablecoins, $801.8 million of 30-day DEX volume, $738,763 of 30-day fees, and $440,499 of 30-day revenue. The stablecoin and trading observations show active rails; they do not by themselves establish payment adoption, institutional settlement, or proportionate APT value capture. Same-day provider values may revise after the stated retrieval time.

why.summary: Observed: Aptos carries far more stablecoin supply and monthly DEX volume than DeFi TVL, while current fees and revenue remain small and TVL is more than 95% below peak. Documented design: it chose Move resources, deterministic Block-STM parallel execution, stake-weighted BFT, separable owner/operator/voter roles, and governance-controlled network parameters rather than EVM compatibility. Strategic inference: this stack is well suited to high-throughput financial rails and lets custodians, operators, and governance voters separate responsibilities, which can help institutional integrations. The same choices do not solve distribution or value capture: a one-million-APT validator minimum raises concentration questions, current documentation says slashing is not implemented, and low-cost throughput can produce impressive activity without much fee burn or native liquidity.

strategic_choices.decision: Use Move resources and Block-STM dynamic parallel execution instead of an EVM-compatible sequential execution environment.
strategic_choices.consequence: Developers can write expressive transactions without predeclaring conflicts and the runtime extracts concurrency, while Aptos must build a separate language, tooling, application, and liquidity ecosystem.

strategic_choices.decision: Separate stake ownership, node operation, and governance voting into distinct onchain roles.
strategic_choices.consequence: Custodians and delegators can assign operational and voting duties without transferring ownership, but beneficial control can be obscured across owners, operators, voters, and staking services.

strategic_choices.decision: Require high stake for direct validation and use stake-weighted leader selection while leaving slashing unimplemented in the documented current design.
strategic_choices.consequence: The model can prioritize a performant professional validator set and reward proposing leaders, but a one-million-APT entry threshold and absent slashing create unresolved concentration and accountability trade-offs.

strategic_choices.decision: Prioritize very low-cost, high-throughput financial activity and change economics through governance and rolling mainnet upgrades.
strategic_choices.consequence: Stablecoin and trading rails can operate cheaply and the implementation can tune fees and performance, while the current gap between activity, TVL, fees, and revenue shows that throughput is not the same as durable capital or APT capture.

counterfactual.summary: EVM compatibility could have reduced developer and liquidity switching costs, but would have abandoned the Move and Block-STM differentiation that defines Aptos. Lower validator stake requirements or implemented slashing might broaden participation or accountability, yet the reviewed sources do not establish their net performance and security effects. Charging more from the beginning could have increased fee capture while weakening the low-cost payments and trading proposition. None of these alternatives is proven to have prevented the 95% TVL drawdown.

watch.signal: Stablecoin supply and DEX volume reconciled with TVL, fees, retained revenue, and identifiable payment flows.
watch.implication: Recurring external settlement with rising revenue would support the financial-rail strategy; high supply and volume without capital retention or fees would preserve the capture gap.

watch.signal: Validator owner, operator, voter, and stake concentration, including the effect of the one-million-APT minimum.
watch.implication: Broad independent control would reduce the concentration concern; a small set of beneficial owners or infrastructure providers would strengthen it.

watch.signal: Mainnet fee, reward, slashing, and performance changes in Aptos Core releases and their measured economic effect.
watch.implication: Governance changes that improve revenue and security without losing recurring usage strengthen the model; parameter churn without improved economics does not.

unknowns.question: What share of Aptos stablecoin flow represents durable external payments or settlement rather than trading, bridging, or incentive routing?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: Counterparty-classified flows, recurring payment cohorts, and independently attributable fees.

unknowns.question: Who beneficially controls validator stake across owner, operator, voter, custodian, and delegation relationships?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: An independent entity-level stake and infrastructure map.

unknowns.question: When, if ever, will slashing be implemented and how would it change validator incentives?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: An enacted governance change and verified mainnet implementation.

unknowns.question: Can Aptos convert high-throughput financial activity into durable APT demand and revenue without pricing out the activity it targets?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A reproducible post-change series for transactions, users, fees, burn, revenue, and retained liquidity.

outcome.label: declining
outcome.summary: Algorand is a declining but operational L1. In the DefiLlama API snapshot fetched at 2026-08-03T17:15:40.082Z, the latest 2026-08-03 historical point was $29.6 million TVL, 90.7% below its February 2024 peak, alongside roughly $37.0 million of dollar stablecoins plus €0.85 million of euro stablecoins, $7.26 million of 30-day DEX volume, $9,465 of 30-day fees, and $3,917 of 30-day revenue. Those figures show a functioning residual economy, but not a self-reinforcing capital, application, or fee base comparable with the network's earlier peak. Same-day provider values may revise after the stated retrieval time.

why.summary: Observed: Algorand remains live with stablecoins and DEX activity, but TVL is more than 90% below peak and monthly fees and revenue are very small. Documented design: cryptographic sortition, fast finality, native protocol primitives, a capped ALGO supply, and low resource requirements produced a technically coherent chain. Strategic inference: those properties did not create the developer, liquidity, and application distribution loop needed to defend share against EVM and other high-throughput ecosystems. Extremely low fees improve user economics but leave little fee-funded security or token capture; Foundation-funded governance and ecosystem incentives supported participation without proving independent demand. The 2025 shift from governance rewards to active proposer rewards and xGov is a rational correction toward security and accountable grants, but current market data does not yet show a durable economic reversal.

strategic_choices.decision: Use cryptographic sortition to select stake-weighted proposers and committees rather than a persistent fixed validator set.
strategic_choices.consequence: Consensus roles are difficult to target before selection and participation can run on modest hardware, while influence still follows online stake and must be measured at the beneficial-owner and infrastructure levels.

strategic_choices.decision: Build bespoke Layer-1 asset, atomic-transfer, and AVM primitives instead of adopting EVM compatibility as the main distribution strategy.
strategic_choices.consequence: Algorand can optimize finality and native operations as one stack, but developers, applications, and liquidity cannot migrate through the dominant EVM toolchain without translation and new ecosystem commitments.

strategic_choices.decision: Keep transaction fees extremely low and subsidize ecosystem participation and rewards from allocated ALGO pools.
strategic_choices.consequence: Users receive cheap execution and the Foundation can bootstrap specific programs, but current fee and revenue totals are too small to demonstrate a self-funding security and application economy independent of finite allocations.

strategic_choices.decision: End rewarded quarterly governance, redirect incentives to active block proposers, and move builder funding toward xGov tied to consensus participation.
strategic_choices.consequence: Rewards align more directly with network security and grant voting can become more accountable, while decaying bonuses, eligibility thresholds, and residual Foundation-operated xGov components remain material dependencies.

counterfactual.summary: Earlier EVM compatibility might have reduced switching costs and improved access to existing applications and liquidity, but could also have diluted the tightly integrated protocol and AVM design; the sources do not prove the net result. Paying active block proposers earlier instead of rewarding passive holders and periodic governors might have strengthened operator incentives sooner. Higher fees could improve direct economic capture while compromising Algorand's low-cost proposition. None of these changes alone would guarantee product distribution, and treating technical quality as sufficient was the more important strategic error.

watch.signal: TVL, stablecoins, DEX volume, fees, and revenue after the shift from governance rewards to staking rewards.
watch.implication: Sustained growth without renewed broad subsidies would support recovery; flat or falling activity would confirm that the incentive redesign improved security mechanics without restoring demand.

watch.signal: Online stake, proposer, relay, hosting, and beneficial-owner concentration under the active reward model.
watch.implication: More independent proposers and infrastructure would validate the decentralization goal; concentration or reward capture by a small set would weaken it.

watch.signal: xGov participation, grant delivery, Foundation-operated components, treasury runway, and follow-on application usage.
watch.implication: Transparent grants that produce recurring users and fees would support a recovery path; governance activity without product outcomes would not.

unknowns.question: Who beneficially controls online stake, block proposals, relays, and the infrastructure behind them?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A current independent entity-level consensus and hosting map.

unknowns.question: Will fee income and decaying proposer bonuses sustain enough independent operators over the long run?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A multi-period model reconciled to onchain fees, rewards, operator costs, and participation.

unknowns.question: How much remaining stablecoin and application activity depends on Foundation incentives or a few counterparties?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: Protocol- and counterparty-level concentration with incentives separated.

unknowns.question: Can xGov-funded public goods create recurring application demand rather than only governance participation?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: Milestone-level grant outcomes linked to retained users, volume, fees, and independent maintenance.
